body: Pretty sure that's not an acceptable solution. GDScript-specific stuff shouldn't be in CodeEdit.
My bad, was able to come up with a better and simpler solution inside `GdScriptEditor`
So I just commented this out, and it seems to still work. No completion directly after `func`. Could you please double check that this is needed, and provide a case were it fails without this code?

It's not that it fails without it, it's that if you don't have this piece of code, it tries to complete the keyword `func` with a user function — that's what I meant with early completion. If the user accepts this completion, `func` gets replaced by the function name, which is unexpected behavior and throws an error for the user.

This piece of code ensures `code-edit` won't try to complete the keyword and replace it if the user accepts its suggestion

When it comes to completion after `func` (i.e, when you add a space after the keyword) in regards to this PR, it works consistently for virtual functions, but it stops working after you override a custom one (maybe not always, but I'll look into it further) 

The reviewed piece of code doesn't cause the issue, though. Tested with and without it, and yielded the same results. 

![bug_not_done](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/e52318a2-6139-4c35-80dc-1848d8406349)


Edit: Added demonstration and clarification, deleted previous comment as I didn't test the issue thoroughly enough and would have to rewrite it either way

v4.5.dev.custom_build [19bb18716] with this PR applied on top. It's worth noting, that I'm only talking about manually triggered completion (`Ctrl + Space`). It doesn't automatically pop up after func since space isn't a trigger character, but that is Editor logic and not related to GDScript. To test GDScript completion code I start with no completion open. Place my cursor where I want it and manually trigger completion.

But I get now what this code is trying to address. It requires a function that contains `func` in its name to actually see the problem.

Personally I don't think we need to handle this edge case in this PR, because this is more like a systematical problem with how completion context works at the moment. E.g. the same problem is present when completing directly after `extends`. But if we work around it I think there is a cleaner approach than relying on source code interaction:

- get the cursor position (can be forwarded from the tokenizer, through gdscript parser)
- if cursor position - completion_context.node.start_column <= 4
    - break

I see, I didn't know there was such a thing as manual autocompletion. I believe I'll be able to replicate your issue now.

This problem also happens when you later add  `@export` to a variable (it replaces `var`), so as you've said, it's a more systematic issue.

Using the parser was my first idea to work around the issue. However, since the methods to getting the `cursor position` are private, I wouldn't be able to get it without making certain variables from the `parser` public, which I don't believe is ideal for an edge case. I believe I could add a getter to the parser for the time being.

I really don't see why the editor code shouldn't have access to the current cursor position. We could easily get it our selfes by looking at the original source code which we give to the parser. But getting it from the parser ensures a single source of truth.

I tried using the parser (and by extension, the tokenizer) in  different ways, and unfortunately, there is a drawback. If you use backspace while writing the function, like in the demonstration bellow, it will still trigger an early autocomplete, as `spaces` and `backspaces` don't really update code completion:

![Cursor approach does not account for backtraces](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/efef9577-c51d-4116-b401-46058b25404e)

Although using the source code might not be the cleanest solution, it is the one that solves the issue consistently and allows both `Ctrl + Space` and `_` while writing code.

If you'd like, I could remove the `substr` and add those invisible characters in the If statement to make the code less 'cluttered'.

Actually, it seems my solution also has its flaws (if you have a callable inside the function, it will still trigger an early completion). I believe this can be solved by looking at the `previous/current` token type and see  if it's a `func` type. If this does not work, I will remove this piece of code and let this be (since it's a more systematic issue).

EDIT: It seems any attempts at solving the problem always have some inconsistencies. (And checking the token's type also does not work). Since this issue cannot be easily circumvented and is part of a bigger problem, I will remove this piece of code.

Note that my suggested solution is more of a workaround. Maybe `Token` should store start/end positions [here](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/be3ecaeb3c51433058ad4e96ec892d18f4291efd/modules/gdscript/gdscript_tokenizer.h#L167-L168) along with the line/column (while `leftmost_column` and `rightmost_column` are pretty useless, and we could also drop `source` since it can be computed via full source code and token start/end position. But that's a significant refactoring, so I'm not asking you to do it in this PR.

This method is probably not needed, since the tokenizer already stores the full source code ([`Tokenizer::source`](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/be3ecaeb3c51433058ad4e96ec892d18f4291efd/modules/gdscript/gdscript_tokenizer.h#L219)). We could add a getter to the tokenizer instead of duplicating the property in the parser (however, strings are COW data, so this is more a question of code elegance and class responsibility than a performance/efficiency issue).

```suggestion
	void parse_function_signature(FunctionNode *p_function, SuiteNode *p_body, const String &p_type, int p_signature_start);
```

We generally do not use `const` when passing primitive types by value. Also, I don't really like adding a new parameter for such a workaround, but I guess it's better than `#ifdef`ing the parameter.

```suggestion
#ifdef TOOLS_ENABLED
	parse_function_signature(function, body, "function", signature_start_pos);
#else // !TOOLS_ENABLED
	parse_function_signature(function, body, "function", -1);
#endif // TOOLS_ENABLED
```
I would move this line even higher, right after the `FunctionNode` allocation.

If we, for example store  `start_pos` in the `current` token. Wouldn't this get reset when `current` changes its type? (E.G from `[` to `]` ) If the value stored in `start_pos` persists, wouldn't this be better stored in the `parser` still?

I guess that adding the source code to the parser makes sense. However, to make it more consistent with how it currently works, IMO adding a getter to the Tokenizer is a solution that stitches together nicely. 

Edit: actually, calling the shots at this is more difficult than I had imagined. On one hand, storing the `source` on the `GDScriptTokenizer` class as a private member, adding a getter function  — this feels more consistent with how parsers work in GDScript as far as I'm concerned. However, this raises a question: why only the child class `GDScriptTokenizerText` has access to the source? would it make sense for the parent to have this as well?

IMO this is okay, since virtual functions also add this when you use autocomplete. We could remove this, but we'd need to add it back on `GDScrpit::Editor` for consistency with virtual's method's autocompletion. Would removing it from the signature be warranted?

body: I thought you changed that, otherwise why would you move the signature assignment before consuming the `:` token, inside `parse_function_signature()`? As for whether to include the colon inside the signature or not, the latter makes sense if we introduce [abstract methods](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/106409).
You can add a virtual method to `GDScriptTokenizer` and override it in `GDScriptTokenizerText`, just like `get_current_position()`.
I think you can leave this workaround as is. Just remove `const` from `const int`.
I don't think we need to do anything in this PR, except maybe add a comment saying "This is a temporary workaround due to the token not storing positions, only lines/columns".

body:
I moved it there to get its token position, i.e where the `:` is located, so the signature ends exactly on that position. If we do it later, after Colon is consumed, some unnecessary characters get added to the signature:



 `func test():`
 ` ‎   ‎ pass`


-  signature above adds the indents before `pass` to itself


 `func test():pass`

- the signature above adds pass to itself as there is not a space after colon so _signature = ():pass_


This in short was making writing any tests impossible

body: Ok, I was wrong here. Then you can leave it as is, or remove the colon here and re-add it in the editor (for future support of abstract methods, or for correctness, since the colon is conceptually not part of the signature, `COLON` + `INDENT` is the syntax for starting a block). Note that you can't go back one _token_ here, since a type specifier can consist of more than one token, instead you need to go back one _character_.
